# Inverses of linear maps and matrices

In the previous section, we saw that many problems that we have encountered can be rephrased as a matrix equation:

$$
Ax = b
$$

where $A$ is a matrix, $x,b$ are columns, and $A,b$ are known but $x$ is unknown.
Let's observe that

$$
Ix = x
$$

where $I$ is the matrix for the identity linear map $I \colon V \to V$ given by $I(v) = v$.

One consequence of this is, if we can find a matrix $B$ such that $BA = I$, then we can apply it to both sides and compute $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Ax =& b \\
BAx =& Bb \\
Ix =& Bb \\
x =& Bb.
\end{aligned}
$$

The quantity on the right is just the matrix $B$ multiplied by the column $b$, which is a multiplication we know how to do, so if we multiply out the right side, we obtain exactly $x$.

Whether such a matrix exists for a particular $A$ is the topic of this chapter.

::: {#exr-trial-inverse}
> Solve the matrix equation
> $$
> \begin{bmatrix}
> 1 & 2 \\
> 2 & 3
> \end{bmatrix}
> \begin{bmatrix}
> x \\
> y
> \end{bmatrix}
> =
> \begin{bmatrix}
> 4  \\
> -1 
> \end{bmatrix}
> $$
> 
> by multiplying (on the left) on both sides of this equation by 
> $$
> \begin{bmatrix}
> -3 & 2 \\
>  2 & -1
> \end{bmatrix}.
> $$
:::

## Identities and inverses

Let's go back and talk about functions $\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ again.
One thing we have for such functions is an identity function
$$
I(x) = x.
$$
We give this the name "identity" and use the symbol $I$ for it, but what in practice does this mean?
What are the properties an identity should have?

::: {#def-identity}
Given a collection $S$ of things and an operation $\cdot : S \times S \to S$ for combining two things in $S$, a *left identity* for $\cdot$ is an element $e \in S$ that satisfies 
$$
e \cdot p = p , \quad \forall p \in S.
$$
A *right identity* for $\cdot$ is an element $\widehat e \in S$ such that
$$
p \cdot \widehat e = p , \quad \forall p \in S.
$$
:::

That is, doing an operation with its left identity on the left side does nothing.
Similarly for the right side.

We have already seen some identity objects so far:

- 0 is a left (and right) identity for $+$ in $\mathbb R$ (or by definition any group, field, etc)
- 1 is a left (and right) identity for multiplication in $\mathbb R$ (or by definition any field, etc)
- the zero vector in a vector space is (by definition) a left (and right) identity for vector addition in that space

The function $I(x) = x$ is a left (and right) identity for a different operation in $\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$; it is the identity for composition.
That is, for any $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$,
$$
I \circ f = f \quad \text{and}\quad  f \circ I = f.
$$
In more detail, this looks like
$$
(I \circ f)(x) = I(f(x)) = f(x) = f(I(x)) = (f \circ I)(x).
$$

If we have an operation and an identity for that operation, we may also be lucky enough to have inverses for that operation:

::: {#def-inverse}
Given a collection $S$ of things and an operation $\cdot : S \times S \to S$ for combining two things in $S$:

- if $\cdot$ has a left identity $e_L$, then an element $p \in S$ has a *left inverse* if there is an element $k \in S$ such that 
  $$
  k \cdot p = e_L.
  $$
- if $\cdot$ has a right identity $e_R$, then an element $p \in S$ has a *right inverse* if there is an element $\widehat k \in S$ such that 
  $$
  p \cdot \widehat k = e_R.
  $$
:::

All the operations we have considered so far have the same left and right inverse, and are associative.
In this case, one can show[^take-abstract-alg] that the left and right inverses, if they exist, are the same.
In this case, we simply call it "the inverse" of (eg) $x$ and write it as $x^{-1}$.

[^take-abstract-alg]: One usually learns to prove this in a course on Abstract Algebra. I have mentioned in an earlier footnote a source for this.

As an example, consider the function $f(x) = x^3 + 1$.
One can check that $g(x)= (x - 1)^{1/3}$ is both a left and right inverse for composition, and so we would normally write $f^{-1} (x) = (x - 1)^{1/3}$.

We have seen other inverse elements:

- Given $a \in \mathbb R$, there is an element (which we usually write $-a$) which is the inverse of $a$ with respect to the operation $+$. 0 is its own inverse w.r.t. $+$.
- Given $a \in \mathbb R$ which is not zero, there is an element (which we usually write $\frac{1}{a}$) which is the inverse of $a$ with respect to the operation $\cdot$. 1 is its own inverse w.r.t. $\cdot$.
- Given a vector $v \in V$ in a vector space, there is (by definition) a vector $-v \in V$ which is an inverse for vector addition.

## The identity for linear functions

If we have a linear function $G : A \to B$, what is the identity for composition?
Well, if there is a left identity $I_L$, it must satisfy $I_L \circ G = G$.
Let's write this out in a diagram:

::: {.imagify zoom='3' }
\usetikzlibrary{matrix}
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em]
  {
     A & B & ? \\};
  \path[-stealth]
    (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$G$} (m-1-2)
    (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$I_L$} (m-1-3)
    ;
  \draw[->,>=stealth] (m-1-1) edge[bend right=30]node[below]{$I_L \circ G = G$} (m-1-3);
\end{tikzpicture}
:::

Since the map on the bottom of the diagram is $G$, we know that the $?$ on the right must be the codomain of $G$, that is, the set $B$:

::: {.imagify zoom='3' }
\usetikzlibrary{matrix}
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em]
  {
     A & B & B \\};
  \path[-stealth]
    (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$G$} (m-1-2)
    (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$I_L$} (m-1-3)
    ;
  \draw[->,>=stealth] (m-1-1) edge[bend right=30]node[below]{$I_L \circ G = G$} (m-1-3);
\end{tikzpicture}
:::

So, $I_L : B \to B$ is a linear function which doesn't change its inputs.
It's straightforward to guess that $I_L (v) = v$.

What about a right inverse $I_R$?
By the same reasoning, 

::: {.imagify zoom='3' }
\usetikzlibrary{matrix}
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em]
  {
     A & A & B \\};
  \path[-stealth]
    (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$I_R$} (m-1-2)
    (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$G$} (m-1-3)
    ;
  \draw[->,>=stealth] (m-1-1) edge[bend right=30]node[below]{$G \circ I_R = G$} (m-1-3);
\end{tikzpicture}
:::

It is straightforward to guess that $I_R(v) = v$ as well.

But beware!
The left and right inverses are not the same function.
$I_L$ has domain and codomain $B$ while $I_R$ has domain and codomain $A$.

However, these two inverses have something on common.
In coordinates, they both have the form
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
the only potential difference is the size.

::: {#def-identity-matrix}
For every vector space $V$ there is an identity function, which is linear, from $V$ to $V$
In general, it takes its input and returns them unmodified:
$$
I(v) = v.
$$

If $V$ is finite dimensional and we fix a basis for it, then $I: F^k \to F^k$.
:::

::: {#lem-identity-mat-in-coords}
In the latter case of @def-identity-matrix, in coordinates $I$ has the form
$$
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::
